content.introduction: The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) controls open market operations, influences the federal funds rate, and sets U.S. monetary policy. It consists of twelve members, including the Board of Governors and rotating Reserve Bank presidents. The FOMC meets regularly to make decisions on monetary policy.
body: The FOMC makes all decisions regarding the conduct of open market operations, which affect the federal funds rate (the rate at which depository institutions lend to each other), the size and composition of the Federal Reserve's asset holdings, and communications with the public about the likely future course of monetary policy. In 1923, they formed the Open Market Investment Committee for these coordinated efforts, which was then transformed into the Open Market Policy Conference in 1930.1 A body called the Federal Open Market Committee was first convened in 1933, following the Glass-Steagall Act; but the FOMC as we know it came into effect only in March of 1936 "as constituted by Section 12A of the Federal Reserve Act as amended by the Banking Act of 1935," as the newly named chairman, Marriner Eccles, explained at that meeting. All members of the Board of Governors and the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York have a permanent voting seat2 on the FOMC; the other 11 Reserve Bank presidents serve on a rotating schedule of one-year terms.

The term "monetary policy" refers to the actions undertaken by a central bank, such as the Federal Reserve, to influence the availability and cost of money and credit to help promote national economic goals. The Federal Reserve controls the three tools of monetary policy--open market operations, the discount rate, and reserve requirements. The Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System is responsible for the discount rate and reserve requirements, and the Federal Open Market Committee is responsible for open market operations. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) consists of twelve members--the seven members of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System; the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York; and four of the remaining eleven Reserve Bank presidents, who serve one-year terms on a rotating basis. #### Federal Reserve Bank Rotation on the FOMC.
